chapter_theme: Doing no hurt holds even when hurt would bring great wealth and even toward those who hurt first. The chapter's ground is self-knowledge, since a person who knows pain in his own life has no reason to inflict it, and it adds that hurt returns to its doer by the same day's end.
structure_note: Going by Parimelazhagar's summary remarks, the chapter forbids hurt done for one's own gain (311), hurt done from enmity (312-314), and hurt done carelessly (315), then hurt generally (316-318), and closes on what it brings the doer (319-320). His glosses for 314-319 are misfiled in this source and have not been used for those verses.

311.reading: Even if it would bring wealth that gives eminence, not hurting others is the settled stand of the stainless.
311.nuance: கோள் is a stance held, not a rule obeyed. The verse puts the temptation first and at its strongest, then refuses it in a word.

positions.position: The prize is the yogic powers such as becoming minute, so the temptation is an ascetic one.
positions.quote: யோகமாகிய சிறப்புத் தரும் அணிமா முதலிய செல்வங்களைப்

positions.position: The prize is ordinary wealth, refused even when it would bring no blame.
positions.quote: இது பழி வாராத செல்வம் பெறினும் தவிர வேண்டு மென்றது.

312.reading: Even when someone in hatred has done them hurt, not hurting in return is the settled stand of the stainless.
312.nuance: Manakkudavar supplies a detail that alters the verse's pairing with 313: here the other person's anger was aroused by one's own fault, whereas 313 treats enmity with no cause. On his view, the two verses together cover both provoked and unprovoked enemies.

positions.position: The attacker has been angered by a fault of one's own.

313.reading: Doing hurt, even to those who hated you though you did nothing, brings sorrow there is no escaping.
313.nuance: The verse chooses the case where retaliation looks most justified, an unprovoked enemy, and says it still rebounds. Parimelazhagar explains the sorrow by an ascetic's loss of austerity and takes the actor to be a renunciant, as Pope's gloss follows him in doing, but the verse doesn't name one.

314.reading: The way to punish those who have hurt you is to shame them by doing them good, and then let it go.
314.nuance: ஒறுத்தல், to punish, is kept: retribution isn't abolished but redefined, and shame remains its instrument, so this isn't quite unconditional love. விடல் adds that one should leave the matter there, without savouring the effect.

315.reading: What comes of understanding, if one doesn't guard against another's pain as one's own?
315.nuance: பிறிதின், 'of another', is neuter and so can reach beyond humans. போற்று is active guarding, so understanding that doesn't produce care is judged to have no result at all.

316.reading: What one has perceived to be painful, one must not come near doing to another.
316.nuance: A negative golden rule, but with உணர்ந்தவை, what has been felt or perceived, as the basis rather than a principle. Pope's couplet says 'his own soul has felt', and Kalaignar too says known through experience, while Manakkudavar only says known.

317.reading: Not doing ill of any degree, at any time, to anyone, with the mind, is the highest thing.
317.nuance: Three universals pile up before the verse arrives at மனத்தானாம், which pulls in two directions. Manakkudavar and Kalaignar extend the ban to harm even in thought, while Pope's 'wilful' and 'knowingly' limit it to harm that is intended.

318.reading: Why does one who knows what is hurtful to his own life do hurtful things to other living beings?
318.nuance: This is posed as a real question and isn't answered. Manakkudavar's touch is that a person differs from unconscious objects in knowing his pain, which is exactly why this conduct is puzzling.

319.reading: If you do hurt to others in the forenoon, hurts to you will come in the afternoon, of themselves.
319.nuance: தாமே, 'of themselves', removes any agent: as Manakkudavar says, nobody else need do it. The speed is rhetorical, since the verse is not a report on timing.

320.reading: All pains rest on those who caused pain; those who want to be without pain cause none.
320.nuance: நோய் occurs four times. Taken strictly, 'all pains' has a hard consequence: anyone who suffers must have caused suffering. Manakkudavar accepts it by a time scheme in which present pain derives from past harm, and in that way this chapter leads into the claim of 330.

positions.position: Present suffering comes from past harm, and harming no one now protects the future.
positions.quote: இக் காலத்து நுகர்கின்ற துன்பமெல்லாம் முற்காலத்துப் பிறர்க் குத் துன்பம் செய்தார் மாட்டே யுளவாம் ;

links.note: Both use ஒறுத்தல், punish. 314 says to punish wrongdoers by shaming them with kindness; 550 says that the king punishing the worst of them with death is simply weeding a crop. The word keeps its form while the ethics of person and state divide.

Both test அறிவு by conduct toward others: 203 calls not harming enemies its peak, and 315 says it comes to nothing without guarding others from pain. Understanding here is measured morally rather than by what one knows.
207 says that the enmity of deeds can't be escaped. 319 adds speed: by the same afternoon. One closes off every direction and the other closes off time.

source_issues: 313-319: Parimelazhagar's glosses are misaligned. The entry for 313 has its own gloss with 314's gloss run on after it; the entries for 314, 315, 316, 317 and 318 hold his glosses for 315, 316, 317, 318 and 319 respectively; and 319 is marked as not aligned. I didn't use his text for 314-319, and only the first part of the entry for 313.
318: the verse text has தன்னுயிர்ககு ஏன்னாமை for தன்னுயிர்க்கு இன்னாமை.
